Population, community, carrying capacity, cycle, reservoir, carbon dioxide, nitrogen gas, fixation, nitrification, phosphate, weathering, sediment, and water processes have local explanations. Bacteria replaces the unexplained prokaryotes term.

Symbiosis effects and signs are defined before #4. Biodiversity, overharvesting, invasive species, and conservation are explained before species-loss and management applications. No prerequisite explanation is needed for the methods used.
Food arrows and branching links explain energy movement; resource limits explain population change; partner benefits and harm explain symbiotic categories.
Carbon is traced through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decay, and burning. Nitrogen processes distinguish gas conversion, ammonium-to-nitrate changes, and return to air.

Phosphorus teaching traces weathering, plant uptake, feeding, decay, runoff, and sediment. Water teaching explains evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, underground return, and transpiration.
Biodiversity consequences are explained through pollinator and food links; conservation actions address distinct damage causes and are checked through monitoring.
The transfer estimate is explicitly conditional on a problem stating it. Consumers may occupy several trophic levels; alternate food sources can soften effects without guaranteeing no change.
Carrying capacity may change, overshoot is possible, and population response can be delayed. Symbiosis labels depend on measured effects rather than appearance.

Nitrogen gas is not directly usable by most plants; phosphorus lacks a major atmospheric gas reservoir. Species-loss effects depend on ecological links; habitat and pollution responses have separate limits.
